examples.question_text:
A fair red four-sided die and a fair blue four-sided die, each numbered $1$ to $4$, are rolled independently. The array records (red, blue).
$\begin{array}{c|cccc}&1&2&3&4\\\hline1&(1,1)&(1,2)&(1,3)&(1,4)\\2&(2,1)&(2,2)&(2,3)&(2,4)\\3&(3,1)&(3,2)&(3,3)&(3,4)\\4&(4,1)&(4,2)&(4,3)&(4,4)\end{array}$
Find, as fractions in simplest form:
(a) the probability of (3,2)
(b) the probability that the sum is at least $7$
(c) the probability of a double
(d) the probability that the sum is $3$ or $8$.
examples.solution_text:
There are $16$ equally likely ordered outcomes.
(a) Only $(3,2)$ matches.
$P((3,2))=\frac{1}{16}$
(b) The favourable cells are $(3,4),(4,3),(4,4)$.
$P(\text{sum at least }7)=\frac{3}{16}$
(c) The doubles are $(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4)$.
$\begin{align*}P(\text{double})&=\frac{4}{16}\\&=\frac{1}{4}\end{align*}$
(d) The favourable cells are $(1,2),(2,1),(4,4)$.
$P(\text{sum }3\text{ or }8)=\frac{3}{16}$

examples.question_text:
Four cards numbered $2,3,5,7$ are shuffled. A card is drawn, recorded and replaced. The cards are shuffled again before a second draw. Every card has the same chance.
(a) Find the probability of drawing a $2$ and a $7$, in any order.
(b) Find the probability of drawing at least one $5$. Give both answers in simplest form.
examples.solution_text:
There are $4\times4=16$ equally likely ordered draws.
(a) The favourable outcomes are $(2,7)$ and $(7,2)$.
$\begin{align*}P(\text{a }2\text{ and a }7)&=\frac{2}{16}\\&=\frac{1}{8}\end{align*}$
(b) The favourable outcomes are $(5,2),(5,3),(5,5),(5,7),(2,5),(3,5),(7,5)$.
Count $(5,5)$ only once.
$P(\text{at least one }5)=\frac{7}{16}$

The eight paths are equally likely.
(a) Exactly two tails occur on $HTT,THT,TTH$.
$P(\text{exactly two tails})=\frac{3}{8}$
(b) Three tails occur only on $TTT$.
$P(\text{three tails})=\frac{1}{8}$

examples.question_text:
Four separate cards are labelled $A_1,A_2,B,C$. The first two both show the letter A. Two cards are chosen in order without replacement, each available card having the same chance.
The array records the individual cards:
$\begin{array}{c|cccc}&A_1&A_2&B&C\\\hline A_1&\times&A_1A_2&A_1B&A_1C\\A_2&A_2A_1&\times&A_2B&A_2C\\B&BA_1&BA_2&\times&BC\\C&CA_1&CA_2&CB&\times\end{array}$
Find, as fractions in simplest form:
(a) the probability that both cards show A
(b) the probability of an A then B
(c) the probability of an A and B, in any order
(d) the probability that the cards show different letters.
examples.solution_text:
Exclude the $4$ crossed-out cells, leaving $12$ equally likely ordered card draws.
(a) Both cards show A on $A_1A_2$ and $A_2A_1$.
$\begin{align*}P(AA)&=\frac{2}{12}\\&=\frac{1}{6}\end{align*}$
(b) An A then B occurs on $A_1B$ and $A_2B$.
$\begin{align*}P(AB)&=\frac{2}{12}\\&=\frac{1}{6}\end{align*}$
(c) The favourable draws are $A_1B,A_2B,BA_1,BA_2$.
$\begin{align*}P(\text{an A and B})&=\frac{4}{12}\\&=\frac{1}{3}\end{align*}$
(d) The different-letter draws are $A_1B,A_1C,A_2B,A_2C,BA_1,BA_2,BC,CA_1,CA_2,CB$.
$\begin{align*}P(\text{different letters})&=\frac{10}{12}\\&=\frac{5}{6}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A fair coin is tossed twice. Lee says, 'The results are two heads, two tails or one of each, so the probability of two heads is $\frac{1}{3}$.' Explain the mistake and find the correct probability.
examples.solution_text:
The equally likely outcomes are $HH,HT,TH,TT$.
One of each occurs in two outcomes, $HT$ and $TH$, so the three results Lee names are not equally likely.
Only $HH$ gives two heads.
$P(\text{two heads})=\frac{1}{4}$

examples.question_text:
Two fair six-sided dice are rolled independently. The table records their sums.
$\begin{array}{c|cccccc}+&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\3&4&5&6&7&8&9\\4&5&6&7&8&9&10\\5&6&7&8&9&10&11\\6&7&8&9&10&11&12\end{array}$
(a) Find the probability of a sum of $9$, as a fraction in simplest form.
(b) Jo says, 'There are eleven possible sums, so the probability of a sum of $9$ is $\frac{1}{11}$.' Explain the mistake.
examples.solution_text:
(a) There are $6\times6=36$ equally likely ordered outcomes. A sum of $9$ occurs on $(3,6),(4,5),(5,4),(6,3)$.
$\begin{align*}P(\text{sum }9)&=\frac{4}{36}\\&=\frac{1}{9}\end{align*}$
(b) The sums are not equally likely. For example, a sum of $2$ occurs in one cell, while a sum of $9$ occurs in four cells. Count the equally likely cells.

examples.derivation: The 4×4 array contains 16 equally likely ordered pairs. There is one (3,2), three pairs with sum at least 7, four doubles, and three pairs with sum 3 or 8. The answers are 1/16, 3/16, 1/4 and 3/16.
Replacement gives 16 equally likely ordered draws. Two contain 2 and 7 in either order, giving 1/8. Four begin with 5 and four end with 5; counting (5,5) once leaves seven, giving 7/16.

Three independent fair tosses give 2×2×2=8 equally likely complete paths: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH and TTT. Exactly two tails occur on HTT, THT and TTH, giving 3/8; three tails occur only on TTT, giving 1/8. The TikZ branches generate these eight outcomes in matching rows. Toss 3 remains at x=4.5 and Outcome moves to x=6.4, with every outcome centred beneath it. This separates the headings without changing branch geometry, mathematics or declared 10 pt labels. The method matches the supplied three-toss investigation and three-question tree exercise.

Without replacement there are 4×3=12 equally likely ordered individual-card draws. Both A and A then B each have two favourable draws; A and B in either order has four. Only the two AA draws have matching letters, leaving ten different-letter draws. The answers are 1/6, 1/6, 1/3 and 5/6.

The sum table contains 36 equally likely ordered outcomes. Sum 9 occurs at (3,6), (4,5), (5,4) and (6,3), giving 4/36=1/9. Sum 2 has one outcome, confirming that the eleven distinct sums are not equally likely.
